Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best way to check guests into an event?

The best method depends on your event size and requirements. Small events may use a printed guest list, while larger events can benefit from digital registration and QR code guest passes. Whichever method you choose, prepare a clear verification and issue-resolution process.

How many registration staff do I need for an event?

This depends on expected attendance, arrival patterns and the time required to verify each guest. Estimate how many people may arrive during your busiest period, then provide enough staff and registration points to handle that volume with some extra capacity.

How do I reduce long queues at event registration?

Open registration early, use clearly labelled desks, separate guest categories where necessary, train your staff and use an efficient verification process. You should also prepare a separate point for resolving registration problems so that one difficult case does not delay everyone.

How do I handle guests who are not on the registration list?

Ask for their registration details, check alternative spellings and refer unresolved cases to an authorised supervisor. Establish an approval process for unexpected guests before the event begins.

Can QR codes be used for event check-in?

What should be included in an event check-in checklist?

Include the final guest list, registration desk arrangement, staff assignments, guest verification process, equipment testing, signage, backup arrangements and procedures for late or unexpected guests.

How early should event registration open?

This depends on the event programme and expected attendance. For many conferences and corporate events, opening registration 30 to 60 minutes before the programme starts can provide a useful arrival window. Larger events may need an earlier opening period.

title: How to Price Event Tickets and Plan Ticket Tiers: A Guide for Event Organisers in Nigeria
excerpt: Calculate event ticket prices, set Early Bird and VIP tiers, estimate break-even sales and plan for different ticket-sales outcomes.
imageAlt: Microphone on stage at a live event
author: Ariya Journal
content:
Introduction

Charge too much, and potential attendees may decide the event is not worth the cost. Charge too little, and you may sell out but still struggle to cover your expenses.

For event organisers in Nigeria, ticket pricing requires careful consideration of venue costs, catering, speakers, marketing, logistics, expected attendance and the amount your target audience is willing to pay.

Whether you are organising a concert, conference, business seminar, networking event, workshop or entertainment experience, your ticket price should reflect both the cost of delivering the event and the value attendees will receive.

One way to approach this is through event ticket tiers. Instead of charging everyone the same amount, you can offer different ticket categories such as Early Bird, Regular, VIP and Group tickets.

This guide explains how to calculate event ticket prices, create ticket tiers, estimate your break-even point and avoid common pricing mistakes.

1. Start With Your Total Event Budget

Before deciding how much attendees should pay, calculate how much it will cost to organise the event.

Your ticket price should not be based on what another organiser charges or what you think people might be willing to pay. It should begin with a realistic understanding of your expenses.

Common event expenses include:

  • Venue: hall rental, event space and deposits.
  • Production: stage, lighting, sound and screens.
  • Speakers and performers: appearance fees, accommodation and transport.
  • Catering: food, drinks and refreshments.
  • Marketing: advertising, content and promotion.
  • Staffing, logistics, technology and contingency costs.

For example:

  • Illustrative ₦3,000,000 event budget: venue ₦800,000; production and equipment ₦650,000; speakers and entertainment ₦400,000; catering ₦450,000; marketing ₦250,000; staffing and logistics ₦200,000; branding ₦100,000; contingency ₦150,000. These estimates total ₦3,000,000 and will vary by event.

Your estimated event budget is ₦3 million. This is the starting point for determining how much revenue you need to generate.

2. Determine How Many Tickets You Can Sell

Venue capacity is not the same as paid ticket capacity. For example, a 300-person venue may need spaces reserved for staff, speakers, production and complimentary guests.

For a clear planning example, allocate 30 spaces for staff and operations and 30 complimentary places. That leaves 240 tickets available for paid sale. You could divide those paid tickets into 200 general-admission tickets and 40 VIP tickets. Use the paid capacity—not the venue's full capacity—in your break-even calculation.

3. Calculate Your Break-Even Ticket Price

Your break-even point is the amount of revenue you need to cover your event expenses.

If your event costs ₦3 million and you have 240 tickets available, simply dividing the budget by the number of tickets gives you an initial estimate.

Break-even ticket price = Total event costs ÷ Number of paid tickets available

Using the example:

₦3,000,000 ÷ 240 = ₦12,500.

This means you would need an average ticket revenue of ₦12,500 per paid attendee to cover the estimated event costs, assuming all 240 tickets are sold and there are no other revenue sources or deductions.

However, this calculation becomes more useful when you include sponsorships and other income.

Include sponsorship and other revenue

Suppose your event has:

  • Total expenses: ₦3,000,000.
  • Confirmed sponsorship income: ₦500,000.
  • Available paid tickets: 240.

Your remaining revenue requirement is:

₦3,000,000 − ₦500,000 = ₦2,500,000.

Your revised break-even average ticket price becomes:

₦2,500,000 ÷ 240 = approximately ₦10,417.

This shows how sponsorship can reduce the amount you need to earn from ticket sales.

Only include sponsorship income that is reasonably confirmed. Do not base your ticket pricing on sponsorship promises that may not materialise.

4. Understand the Different Types of Event Ticket Tiers

Ticket tiers allow you to offer different prices and experiences to different categories of attendees.

Instead of charging one price throughout the sales period, you can create a structured pricing model.

Here are some common ticket categories.

Early Bird Tickets

Early Bird tickets are discounted tickets made available during the initial sales period.

They encourage people to commit early and help organisers generate initial revenue.

For example:

  • Early Bird: ₦8,000.
  • Regular: ₦12,000.

Early Bird tickets should have a clear quantity limit or closing date.

Do not make them available indefinitely. If the discounted price never ends, attendees may have little reason to purchase at the regular price.

Regular Tickets

Regular tickets are the standard admission option.

They are usually available after the Early Bird period ends and remain the main ticket category for the event.

For example:

  • Regular admission: ₦12,000.

Your regular price should be based on your costs, audience expectations and the value of the event.

VIP Tickets

VIP tickets cost more because they provide additional benefits beyond standard admission.

Depending on your event, these benefits could include:

  • Reserved seating.
  • Access to a VIP lounge.
  • Priority registration.
  • Exclusive networking opportunities.
  • Special refreshments.
  • Premium event materials.
  • Meet-and-greet opportunities, where applicable.

For example:

  • Regular admission: ₦12,000.
  • VIP admission: ₦25,000.

The difference in price should be supported by a genuine difference in experience.

Do not create a VIP category simply because you want to charge more. Clearly explain what additional value attendees receive.

Group Tickets

Group tickets allow multiple people to register or attend at a reduced combined price.

For example:

  • Individual ticket: ₦12,000.
  • Group of five: ₦55,000.

This means each person in the group effectively pays ₦11,000.

Group pricing can encourage teams, friends, colleagues and business partners to attend together.

However, ensure that the discount does not reduce your average revenue below a sustainable level.

Student or Special Category Tickets

For educational conferences, workshops and professional development events, you may want to offer discounted tickets to students or specific groups.

These tickets should have clearly defined eligibility requirements.

For example, student attendees may be required to provide a valid student identification document during registration or check-in.

5. How to Structure Your Ticket Tiers

Creating ticket categories is not enough. You need to determine how many tickets to allocate to each category and when each price should be available.

For a separate illustration of ticket-tier revenue, assume a business conference has 200 paid tickets available. This example is not the 240-ticket venue-capacity scenario above.

  • Early Bird: 40 tickets at ₦8,000 = ₦320,000.
  • Regular: 130 tickets at ₦12,000 = ₦1,560,000.
  • VIP: 30 tickets at ₦25,000 = ₦750,000.
  • If all 200 tickets in this separate example sell, gross ticket revenue is ₦2,630,000 before applicable fees, refunds or other deductions.

₦2,630,000If every ticket sells, the event generates ₦2.63 million in ticket revenue before applicable fees, refunds or other deductions.

If the event also receives ₦500,000 in confirmed sponsorship income, its total revenue would be ₦3.13 million.

Against the illustrative ₦3 million event budget, that leaves ₦130,000 before any additional costs or deductions not already included in the budget.

This example demonstrates why ticket pricing should be calculated across all categories rather than treating each ticket price independently.

It also shows why a high VIP price does not automatically make an event profitable. The quantity of tickets sold in each category matters.

6. Consider Your Target Audience and the Value of the Event

Your expenses are important, but they should not be the only factor influencing your ticket price.

You also need to consider what your target audience is willing to pay.

A business conference attended by senior professionals may justify a higher ticket price if it provides valuable speakers, industry insights, networking opportunities and practical learning.

A community networking event or student workshop may require a different pricing approach.

Consider these questions:

Who is your target audience?

Are you selling to students, young professionals, business owners, executives, families or entertainment enthusiasts?

What problem or need does the event address?

An event that offers practical training, professional certification or access to industry leaders may provide more measurable value than a general social gathering.

What does the ticket include?

Does the price cover meals, refreshments, materials, networking, entertainment or additional experiences?

What alternatives are available?

Consider other events targeting the same audience and how your event compares in terms of quality, location, speakers and benefits.

Your goal is to set a price that makes commercial sense while remaining reasonable for your intended audience.

7. Account for Payment and Other Selling Costs

One mistake event organisers make is assuming that the amount paid by attendees is the same as the amount they will receive.

Depending on the ticketing and payment arrangements, there may be transaction charges, platform fees, taxes or other deductions.

For example, if an attendee pays ₦20,000 for a ticket and the applicable transaction costs are ₦500, the organiser may receive less than the original ticket price.

Before launching ticket sales, establish:

  • Whether payment processing fees apply.
  • Whether the organiser or buyer bears those fees.
  • Whether any platform charges apply.
  • When ticket-sale proceeds are made available.
  • Whether taxes or other statutory obligations apply.
  • How cancellations and refunds are handled.

Do not assume every ticketing platform has the same pricing or payout arrangement.

If you are using a ticketing platform, confirm its current terms before setting your final prices or advertising payment arrangements.

8. Decide When to Increase Your Ticket Prices

A structured ticket release can encourage early purchases and create a reason for attendees to register sooner.

A common approach is to use three sales periods.

Sales periodTicket categoryExample priceInitial launchEarly Bird₦8,000Main sales periodRegular₦12,000Final sales periodLate Registration₦15,000This structure rewards people who commit early while reflecting the shorter time available for late registrations.

However, price increases should be communicated clearly.

If you announce that Early Bird tickets will end on a particular date, honour that deadline. Repeatedly extending a supposedly limited offer can reduce trust and make future deadlines less meaningful.

Also, consider whether a final price increase is appropriate for your audience. A higher late-registration price should be part of your pricing strategy, not simply a last-minute attempt to generate more money.

9. Plan for Complimentary Tickets and Discounts

Not every attendee will necessarily purchase a ticket.

You may need to reserve complimentary access for:

  • Speakers.
  • Sponsors.
  • Media representatives.
  • Special guests.
  • Event partners.
  • Internal staff.

You may also want to offer promotional discounts to selected groups.

The important thing is to include these allocations in your event budget and capacity planning.

For example, if your venue accommodates 300 people and you reserve 30 spaces for complimentary guests and operations, you cannot plan to sell 300 paid tickets.

Also, record complimentary tickets separately from paid tickets. This allows you to understand the difference between total attendance and actual ticket revenue.

10. Common Event Ticket Pricing Mistakes to Avoid

Pricing tickets without calculating costs

Choosing a price because it sounds affordable can leave you unable to cover your expenses.

Ignoring venue capacity

Planning ticket sales beyond your actual sellable capacity can create overcrowding and operational problems.

Offering too many ticket categories

Too many options can confuse potential attendees. Keep your categories simple and make the differences clear.

Setting VIP prices without additional value

Attendees should understand why a VIP ticket costs more and what they receive in return.

Discounting tickets too frequently

Constant discounts can make people question the original price and delay purchasing.

Forgetting transaction costs

The gross ticket price may not be the final amount received by the organiser.

Ignoring unsold ticket risk

Your financial plan should not depend entirely on selling every available ticket. Consider what happens if only 60%, 70% or 80% of tickets sell.

Failing to communicate ticket conditions

Clearly explain ticket benefits, eligibility, sales deadlines, transfer conditions and applicable refund policies before people purchase.

11. How to Calculate Whether Your Event Will Be Profitable

After determining your ticket prices, estimate the revenue your event could generate at different sales levels.

Consider the following example:

  • Total event expenses: ₦3,000,000.
  • Confirmed sponsorship: ₦500,000.
  • Ticket revenue if sold out: ₦2,630,000.

Your projected total revenue is ₦3,130,000.

Your projected surplus is ₦130,000 before additional deductions or unbudgeted costs.

But what happens if not every ticket sells?

  • At 100 tickets sold: ₦1,315,000 ticket revenue plus ₦500,000 sponsorship = ₦1,815,000 total, or ₦1,185,000 below the ₦3,000,000 budget.
  • At 140 tickets: ₦2,341,000 total revenue, or ₦659,000 below budget.
  • At 180 tickets: ₦2,867,000 total revenue, or ₦133,000 below budget.
  • At 200 tickets: ₦3,130,000 total revenue, or ₦130,000 above budget before additional deductions.

These estimates assume the same ticket mix at each sales level.

This exercise helps you understand your financial exposure before committing to the event.

You should also calculate a more conservative scenario in which sponsorship is lower, expenses increase or sales are slower than expected.

12. A Practical Event Ticket Pricing Checklist

Before publishing your tickets, confirm the following:

Budget and Capacity

  • Total event expenses calculated.
  • Contingency included.
  • Sponsorship and other revenue identified.
  • Venue capacity confirmed.
  • Sellable ticket quantity established.
  • Complimentary allocations deducted.

Ticket Categories

  • Early Bird price established.
  • Regular ticket price established.
  • VIP benefits and price defined.
  • Group or special-category discounts considered.
  • Ticket quantities allocated.
  • Sales periods and deadlines established.

Financial Planning

  • Break-even ticket revenue calculated.
  • Payment and platform charges checked.
  • Refund and cancellation arrangements reviewed.
  • Conservative sales forecast prepared.
  • Profitability scenarios reviewed.

Sales Preparation

  • Ticket descriptions written clearly.
  • Ticket conditions communicated.
  • Registration and payment process tested.
  • Ticket confirmation process reviewed.
  • Guest communication plan prepared.

Manage Your Event Registration and Guest Passes with AriyaHQ

Once your ticket prices and categories are established, you need an organised way to manage the people attending your event.

AriyaHQ helps event organisers manage important guest-facing activities, including:

  • Digital event invitations.
  • Online registration and RSVP management.
  • Guest list organisation.
  • Bulk SMS and bulk email communication.
  • Unique QR code guest passes.

These capabilities can support the registration and guest management side of your event, helping you organise attendee information before event day.

If you are planning a paid conference, seminar, workshop or other event, explore AriyaHQ to see how it can support your event management process.

Important: Confirm AriyaHQ's current paid-ticket creation, payment collection, transaction fee and payout capabilities before relying on it as your ticket sales or payment-processing solution.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I calculate the price of an event ticket?

Start by calculating your total event expenses, subtract confirmed sponsorship and other revenue, and divide the remaining amount by the number of paid tickets you realistically expect to sell. Then consider payment costs, audience affordability and the value of the event.

What is an Early Bird ticket?

An Early Bird ticket is a discounted ticket offered during the initial sales period. It encourages attendees to register early and gives organisers an opportunity to generate initial revenue.

What is the difference between Regular and VIP tickets?

Regular tickets generally provide standard event admission, while VIP tickets offer additional benefits such as reserved seating, priority access, exclusive networking or special refreshments.

How many ticket categories should an event have?

There is no fixed number, but most events can start with two or three clearly defined categories, such as Early Bird, Regular and VIP. Add other categories only when they serve a genuine audience or business need.

Should event organisers charge more for late registration?

They can, provided the pricing structure is communicated in advance and the higher price is reasonable for the audience and event. Late pricing can reflect increased preparation costs and the benefit of purchasing earlier.

What happens if an event does not sell all its tickets?

Unsold tickets reduce the revenue available to cover event expenses. Organisers should prepare different sales forecasts before the event and avoid depending entirely on selling out to remain financially sustainable.

Should ticket processing fees be included in the ticket price?

That depends on the payment arrangement and the applicable platform terms. Organisers should establish who bears the fees and communicate the final amount payable to attendees clearly.

Can I offer free and paid tickets for the same event?

Yes. Some events offer free registration for selected categories while charging for VIP access, workshops or premium experiences. Ensure that free allocations are included in your capacity and financial planning.

title: Event Promotion: A Week-by-Week Marketing Timeline for Event Organisers
excerpt: Follow an eight-week event promotion timeline, from the first announcement through attendee follow-up after the event.
imageAlt: Event organisers planning a promotion together around a table
author: Ariya Journal
content:
Introduction

Whether you are organising a conference, wedding, concert, business seminar, product launch, workshop or networking event, people need to hear about it, understand why they should attend and have enough time to make a decision.

The challenge for many event organisers is knowing what to promote, when to promote it and how frequently to communicate with their audience.

Start too late, and you may struggle to attract enough attendees. Promote too aggressively too early, and people may lose interest before the event takes place.

The solution is to work with a structured event marketing timeline.

This guide provides an eight-week event promotion plan that shows what to do at each stage, what content to publish, when to send invitations and how to turn interest into registrations.

It also explains how AriyaHQ can support the communication and guest-management side of your campaign through digital invitations, registration, RSVP management, bulk SMS and bulk email.

Before You Start: Prepare Your Event Marketing Foundation

Before launching your campaign, make sure the important details are ready.

You should know:

  • Event name and purpose.
  • Event date and time.
  • Venue or online attendance details.
  • Target audience.
  • Ticket or registration information.
  • Speakers, performers or key participants.
  • Main benefits of attending.
  • Registration deadline, where applicable.
  • Contact details for enquiries.

You should also establish what you want your promotion to achieve.

For example, your objectives might include:

  • Generating 500 registrations.
  • Selling 300 paid tickets.
  • Attracting 50 corporate delegates.
  • Getting 100 people to register for a product launch.
  • Increasing awareness of a new event brand.

Your marketing activities should support these objectives.

Important: Do not measure campaign success only by likes, comments or followers. Registrations, ticket sales, attendance and other meaningful outcomes matter more.

For a broader overview of promotion channels and event marketing, see our event promotion guide.

The Eight-Week Event Promotion Timeline

The timeline below assumes your event is eight weeks away. For smaller events, you can shorten it. For major conferences and large public events, you may need to begin much earlier.

Week 8: Establish Your Campaign and Announce the Event

Campaign launch

The first week is about making your audience aware that the event is happening.

You do not need to publish every detail immediately, but you should communicate enough information to generate interest and give people a reason to pay attention.

What to do

  1. Finalise your event name, date and venue.
  2. Identify your target audience.
  3. Prepare your main event announcement.
  4. Create your promotional graphics and videos.
  5. Set up your registration or ticket information.
  6. Prepare your event communication channels.
  7. Publish the official announcement.

Content to publish

  • Event announcement flyer.
  • Short introductory video.
  • Announcement from the organiser.
  • Social media post explaining what the event is about.
  • Website or registration page announcement.

Example announcement

"Something exciting is coming!

Join us for [Event Name], an experience designed to bring together [target audience] for [main purpose or benefit].

Date: [Event Date]

Venue: [Event Venue]

Registration is now open. Secure your place today."

What to measure

  • Announcement reach.
  • Website or registration page visits.
  • Initial registrations.
  • Enquiries and expressions of interest.

AriyaHQ connection: If you are managing invited guests, prepare your digital invitations and registration process with AriyaHQ so that interested attendees have a clear way to respond.

Week 7: Introduce the Value of the Event

Build interest

After announcing the event, explain why people should attend.

An event announcement tells people that something is happening. Your next task is to convince them that the experience is worth their time and money.

Focus on the value attendees will receive.

What to do

  • Introduce the main event theme.
  • Explain the problems the event addresses.
  • Highlight key activities.
  • Share the benefits of attending.
  • Introduce confirmed speakers or performers, where applicable.
  • Publish answers to common questions.

Content to publish

  • "Why you should attend" posts.
  • Speaker introduction graphics.
  • Event highlights.
  • Short videos explaining the event's purpose.
  • Previous event photographs or testimonials, if available.

For a business conference, you might explain what participants will learn, who they will meet and what practical knowledge they will take away.

For a concert, you might highlight the performers, atmosphere and experience.

What to measure

  • Engagement on event-related posts.
  • Registration growth.
  • Questions from potential attendees.
  • Clicks to the registration page.

Week 6: Expand Your Reach Through Partnerships

At this stage, begin reaching audiences beyond your existing followers.

Your event may have a strong following among people who already know your organisation, but partnerships can introduce it to new communities.

What to do

  • Contact relevant influencers and content creators.
  • Ask speakers to share the event with their audiences.
  • Approach industry associations and professional communities.
  • Contact brand partners and sponsors.
  • Identify organisations that can distribute your event announcement.
  • Explore relevant community and media partnerships.

Content to publish

  • Partner announcement graphics.
  • Speaker collaboration videos.
  • Influencer event announcements.
  • Joint promotional posts.
  • Behind-the-scenes content.

Do not approach influencers simply because they have a large following. Consider whether their audience matches the people you want to attract.

A smaller creator with a highly relevant audience may generate more registrations than a much larger creator with little connection to your event.

What to measure

  • Referral traffic.
  • Registrations from partner channels.
  • Engagement on collaborative posts.
  • Cost per registration for paid partnerships.

Week 5: Start a Strong Content and Advertising Push

By now, people should understand what the event is about. This is a good time to increase the frequency and variety of your promotional content.

If your budget allows, begin testing paid advertising.

What to do

  • Run targeted social media advertisements.
  • Publish short-form videos.
  • Share speaker or performer interviews.
  • Highlight the event's most attractive features.
  • Retarget people who have previously engaged with your campaign, where your advertising setup supports it.
  • Review which promotional messages generate the most registrations.

Content to publish

  • Short promotional reels.
  • Speaker interviews.
  • Event preparation videos.
  • Testimonials from previous attendees.
  • Programme highlights.
  • Registration reminders.

Do not spend your entire advertising budget immediately.

Test different messages and audiences, monitor the results and invest more in the combinations that generate meaningful registrations.

What to measure

  • Advertising spend.
  • Cost per registration.
  • Click-through rate.
  • Registration conversion rate.
  • Performance by advertising channel.

Week 4: Create Urgency and Address Registration Objections

Four weeks before the event, your campaign should begin shifting from general awareness to encouraging people to commit.

Some people may already be interested but have not registered because they are waiting for more information.

Others may be unsure whether they can attend.

Your job is to remove unnecessary uncertainty.

What to do

  • Share the full event programme.
  • Explain ticket categories and what each includes.
  • Highlight important speakers and activities.
  • Answer questions about venue, parking, access and timing.
  • Publish genuine registration deadlines.
  • Share relevant testimonials or previous event results.

Content to publish

  • Full programme announcement.
  • Venue information.
  • Ticket or registration guide.
  • Frequently asked questions.
  • Countdown graphics.
  • Previous attendee testimonials.

If you are using Early Bird pricing, remind your audience when the offer ends.

Only communicate limited ticket quantities or deadlines when they are genuine.

What to measure

  • Registrations during the week.
  • Ticket category performance.
  • Frequently asked questions.
  • Abandoned registration enquiries, where measurable.

Week 3: Strengthen Direct Communication

Social media is useful for awareness, but it should not be your only communication channel.

At this stage, organise direct communication with people who have already shown interest, registered or received invitations.

Different groups need different messages.

For example:

  • Registered attendees: confirmation and practical event information.
  • Invited guests awaiting a response: an RSVP reminder.
  • Interested prospects: event benefits and registration details.
  • Speakers, sponsors and partners: programme and coordination updates.
  • Previous attendees: an invitation to attend again.

Using AriyaHQ for event communication

AriyaHQ supports organisers with digital invitations, RSVP management, bulk SMS and bulk email.

Instead of sending every communication individually, organisers can use bulk messaging to reach larger guest lists.

For example, you can prepare:

  • Registration confirmation messages.
  • RSVP follow-ups.
  • Programme announcements.
  • Event information emails.
  • Important attendee updates.

Keep your messages relevant to the recipient's status. Someone who has already registered should not keep receiving messages asking them to register.

What to measure

  • Registration conversion.
  • Email engagement, where available.
  • SMS delivery information, where available.
  • RSVP response rate.
  • Enquiries generated by direct communication.

Week 2: Focus on Confirmations and Practical Event Information

With two weeks remaining, shift more attention towards people who are expected to attend.

Your communication should now help attendees prepare for the actual event.

What to do

  • Confirm registration information.
  • Share the venue address and directions.
  • Explain arrival times.
  • Publish the final programme.
  • Remind guests about registration requirements.
  • Reconfirm important arrangements with speakers and partners.
  • Review ticket and registration numbers against your targets.

Content to publish

  • "Two weeks to go" announcement.
  • Venue and directions video.
  • Final programme graphic.
  • Speaker confirmation posts.
  • Event preparation updates.
  • Attendee information post.

For events with invited guests, this is also a good time to review outstanding RSVPs and follow up with people who have not responded.

Do not confuse someone who received an invitation with someone who has confirmed attendance.

What to measure

  • Confirmed attendance.
  • Outstanding RSVPs.
  • Ticket sales against available capacity.
  • Attendance information that still needs to be communicated.

Week 1: Run Your Final Promotion Push

Final campaign week

The final week is about converting remaining interest, confirming attendance and ensuring people have the information they need.

Avoid making major changes to the event unless necessary. Your priority should be to communicate clearly and prepare for execution.

What to do

  • Publish daily or near-daily countdown content where appropriate.
  • Share final registration information.
  • Send reminders to confirmed attendees.
  • Confirm speaker and vendor arrangements.
  • Review the guest list.
  • Prepare registration staff and guest passes.
  • Confirm event-day communication responsibilities.

Content to publish

  • Seven-day countdown.
  • Three-day countdown.
  • Final registration reminder.
  • Event preparation videos.
  • Final speaker or performer announcements.
  • Venue directions.
  • Event-day information.

Sample final reminder

"One week to go!

We're getting ready for [Event Name], and we look forward to welcoming you.

Date: [Event Date]

Time: [Event Time]

Venue: [Event Venue]

If you haven't registered yet, complete your registration before the deadline.

For confirmed attendees, please keep your registration details or guest pass accessible for arrival."

What to measure

  • Final registrations.
  • Remaining ticket availability.
  • Confirmed attendance.
  • Guest communication completion.
  • Outstanding event-day arrangements.

Event Day: Keep Communication Active

Promotion does not necessarily stop when the event begins.

You may still need to communicate with attendees, provide directions and share important updates.

What to do

  • Publish event-day updates.
  • Share photographs and short videos.
  • Welcome attendees online.
  • Provide directions or important announcements where necessary.
  • Share approved highlights.
  • Encourage attendees to share their experiences.

You can also capture content for future event promotions.

Photographs, short interviews, testimonials and event highlights can become valuable promotional material for your next edition.

What to measure

  • Actual attendance.
  • Registration-to-attendance conversion.
  • Social media mentions.
  • Attendee engagement.
  • Content performance.

After the Event: Turn One Campaign Into the Next

Your marketing work should not end when the event is over.

Post-event communication helps maintain relationships and makes it easier to promote future editions.

Within the days following the event:

  1. Thank attendees, speakers, sponsors and partners.
  2. Share event photographs and approved recordings.
  3. Publish highlights and testimonials.
  4. Request attendee feedback.
  5. Review your campaign performance.
  6. Document the channels that generated the most registrations.
  7. Build an audience for future events, with appropriate consent.

A successful event should give you more than a single day's attendance. It should help you build a community that is interested in what you organise next.

Your Event Promotion Timeline at a Glance

  • Eight weeks before: announce the event and open registration.
  • Seven weeks before: explain the event's value.
  • Six weeks before: activate partners and collaborators.
  • Five weeks before: increase visibility with content and advertising.
  • Four weeks before: answer questions and encourage registration.
  • Three weeks before: follow up with interested audiences.
  • Two weeks before: share practical information and confirmations.
  • One week before: send final reminders and complete preparation.
  • Event day: share updates. Afterward: thank attendees, collect feedback and review results.

How to Know Whether Your Event Promotion Is Working

A campaign can generate thousands of views and still fail to attract enough attendees.

That is why you should monitor results throughout the campaign.

Here are the most useful metrics.

1. Registrations

How many people have registered for the event?

Compare the number against your registration target.

2. Ticket sales

For paid events, track the number of tickets sold and the revenue generated.

3. Registration conversion rate

This measures how many people who visit your registration page actually complete registration.

For example, if 1,000 people visit your registration page and 100 register, your conversion rate is 10%.

4. Cost per registration

Divide your advertising expenditure by the number of registrations generated from that campaign.

For example, if you spend ₦50,000 on advertising and receive 100 registrations, your cost per registration is ₦500.

5. RSVP response rate

For invitation-based events, measure the proportion of invited guests who have responded.

6. Attendance rate

Compare the number of people who actually attend with the number who registered or confirmed.

7. Channel performance

Identify which channels are producing the most valuable results.

An Instagram campaign may generate awareness, while WhatsApp, email or direct invitations may contribute more to actual registrations. Use your available tracking data rather than assuming one channel is always best.

Common Event Promotion Mistakes to Avoid

Starting promotion too late: People need time to discover the event, make arrangements and register.

Publishing only flyers: Use videos, interviews, programme highlights, testimonials and useful information to keep your campaign interesting.

Ignoring direct communication: Social media followers are not the same as registered attendees. Provide clear registration and communication channels.

Promoting without a clear audience: Your message and advertising should be designed for the people most likely to attend.

Sending too many reminders: Repeated messages without useful information can frustrate your audience.

Failing to track registrations: Without tracking, you may continue spending money on campaigns that are not producing results.

Not preparing for the final week: Last-minute communication, registration issues and missing event information can undermine an otherwise successful campaign.

Plan Your Event Communication With AriyaHQ

An event promotion campaign involves more than publishing content. Organisers also need to manage invitations, registrations, attendance confirmations and important updates.

AriyaHQ helps bring these guest-facing activities together.

With AriyaHQ, organisers can:

  • Create and send digital event invitations.
  • Manage online registration and RSVP responses.
  • Organise guest information.
  • Send bulk SMS to communicate important event updates.
  • Send bulk email to larger guest lists.
  • Provide unique QR code guest passes for guest identification and entry management.

For example, you can use social media and advertising to attract attention, direct interested people to your registration process, and use AriyaHQ to support invitations and communication with your guests.

This creates a more organised process between promoting an event and preparing the people who will attend it.

Whether you are planning a conference, workshop, wedding, product launch or corporate event, explore AriyaHQ to simplify your event guest management and communication.

Frequently Asked Questions

How early should I start promoting an event?

For many small and medium-sized events, starting around six to eight weeks ahead provides a useful promotional window. Large conferences, major entertainment events and events involving international speakers may require several months of promotion.

How often should I promote an event?

There is no universal posting frequency. The important thing is to maintain consistent communication without overwhelming your audience. Vary your content and increase the relevance of reminders as the event approaches.

What is the best way to promote an event in Nigeria?

The best approach depends on your audience. Common channels include Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, WhatsApp, email, SMS, partnerships and paid advertising. Combining social media awareness with direct communication and a clear registration process can help turn interest into attendance.

When should I send event reminders?

A practical schedule is to send useful reminders after registration, around two weeks before the event, during the final week and shortly before the event. Adjust the schedule to the event type and avoid sending unnecessary messages.

How much should I spend promoting an event?

Your marketing budget should reflect your event size, audience, ticket price, revenue target and promotional channels. Start with a defined budget, test different campaigns and increase spending on channels that produce meaningful results.

How do I measure event marketing success?

Track registrations, ticket sales, cost per registration, registration conversion, RSVP responses and actual attendance. Social media engagement is useful, but it should not be your only measure of success.

title: Event Budget Template: How to Track Estimated Costs, Actual Expenses and Vendor Payments
excerpt: Build an event budget tracker for estimates, vendor quotes, actual costs, payment deadlines, cash flow and remaining balances.
imageAlt: Couple celebrating at a wedding reception
author: Ariya Journal
content:
Introduction

Without a proper tracking system, it is easy to underestimate expenses, forget outstanding payments or discover too late that your event is costing more than expected.

Whether you are organising a wedding, conference, birthday celebration, corporate event or concert, an event budget template can help you stay organised and make better financial decisions.

In this guide, we will explain how to create an event budget, track vendor payments and monitor actual expenses. You will also find a practical template you can adapt for your next event.

1. What Is an Event Budget?

An event budget is a financial plan that estimates how much money you need to organise an event.

It outlines the different expenses involved, how much you expect to spend on each item and how you intend to manage payments.

A good event budget should help you answer five important questions:

  • How much money is available for the event?
  • What are the expected expenses?
  • How much have vendors quoted?
  • How much has already been paid?
  • How much money is still outstanding?

Your budget should not be a document you prepare once and forget. It should be updated throughout the planning process as vendors are selected, prices change and payments are made.

2. List Every Expense Before Setting Your Budget

Before contacting vendors or making payments, identify the different things your event will require.

The expenses will depend on the type, size and location of your event.

For example, a corporate conference may require a venue, speakers, audiovisual equipment and registration materials. A wedding may require catering, decoration, photography, entertainment and transportation.

Here are common event expense categories:

  • Venue: hall hire, outdoor space and deposits.
  • Catering and serving staff.
  • Decoration, entertainment, photography and video.
  • Audio-visual equipment and speakers.
  • Marketing, communication and printing.
  • Logistics, staffing and guest-management supplies.

Remember to include smaller purchases and delivery costs.

A useful approach is to divide expenses into three groups:

Essential expenses: Items the event cannot happen without, such as the venue, catering or required equipment.

Important expenses: Items that improve the event experience but may have alternatives.

Optional expenses: Extras you can remove or reduce if the budget becomes tight.

This classification helps you make decisions when costs exceed your initial estimates.

3. Create an Event Budget Tracker

Once you have identified your expenses, put them into a spreadsheet.

A useful event budget tracker should do more than list prices. It should show what you expected to spend, what vendors quoted, what you approved, what you have paid and what remains outstanding.

Use the following structure:

  • Venue (ABC Events Centre): estimate ₦500,000; quote and approved budget ₦550,000; paid ₦300,000; balance ₦250,000.
  • Catering (Taste House): estimate ₦800,000; quote and approved budget ₦750,000; paid ₦300,000; balance ₦450,000.
  • Decoration (Creative Spaces): estimate ₦350,000; quote ₦400,000; approved budget ₦380,000; paid ₦200,000; balance ₦180,000.
  • Photography (Lens Studio): estimate ₦200,000; quote and approved budget ₦180,000; paid ₦90,000; balance ₦90,000.
  • Sound and lighting (SoundPro): estimate ₦250,000; quote and approved budget ₦280,000; paid ₦140,000; balance ₦140,000.

All names and figures are illustrative; actual prices vary by event and supplier.

Your tracker should also include these additional columns:

  • Payment due date: When the next payment must be made.
  • Payment status: Not paid, deposit paid, partially paid or fully paid.
  • Priority: High, medium or low.
  • Notes: Agreed terms, changes, additional charges or payment conditions.

The more clearly you record these details, the easier it becomes to understand your financial position.

4. Understand the Difference Between Estimated, Quoted and Actual Costs

One common budgeting mistake is treating every figure as though it means the same thing.

These three figures serve different purposes.

Estimated cost

This is what you expect an item to cost before receiving a vendor's quotation.

For example, you may allocate ₦300,000 for event decoration based on your initial research.

Quoted cost

This is the price a vendor offers to provide the service.

A decorator may quote ₦350,000 after understanding your requirements.

Actual cost

This is the final amount you end up spending.

The actual cost may differ from the quotation if you add services, change your requirements or incur additional charges.

Tracking these figures separately helps you identify where your assumptions were inaccurate and where costs are increasing.

5. Track Vendor Deposits and Outstanding Payments

Many event vendors require an initial deposit before they begin work. Others require payment in stages.

If you only record the total agreed price, you may lose track of how much is due and when it must be paid.

For every vendor, record:

  1. The total agreed amount.
  2. The deposit required.
  3. The amount already paid.
  4. The remaining balance.
  5. The next payment deadline.
  6. Any conditions attached to the payment.

For example:

VendorTotal CostDepositPaid So FarBalanceNext Due DateVenue₦550,000₦200,000₦300,000₦250,00010 DecemberCaterer₦750,000₦250,000₦300,000₦450,00015 DecemberDecorator₦380,000₦150,000₦200,000₦180,00018 DecemberExample figures and dates only.

Update the tracker immediately after every payment. Keep payment receipts and written confirmations so you can verify transactions when necessary.

Important: Do not assume that paying a deposit automatically secures every service or date. Confirm the vendor's cancellation, refund and rescheduling terms in writing before transferring money.

6. Include a Contingency Fund

No matter how carefully you plan, unexpected expenses can arise.

A vendor may increase a price, transportation may cost more than expected, or you may need additional equipment shortly before the event.

This is why your budget should include a contingency fund.

A practical starting point is to reserve around 5%–10% of your estimated event expenses, adjusting the amount based on the event's complexity and uncertainty.

For example, if your planned event expenses are ₦5,000,000:

  • Planned expenses: ₦5,000,000
  • 5% contingency: ₦250,000
  • 10% contingency: ₦500,000

Your total funding target would therefore be between ₦5,250,000 and ₦5,500,000.

Keep this money separate from your regular spending allocation. Do not use it for optional upgrades unless you have reviewed the remaining budget.

7. Monitor Your Budget With These Three Calculations

A budget becomes more useful when you can measure how much you have spent and how much remains.

Here are three calculations every event organiser should understand.

A. Outstanding vendor balance

This shows how much you still owe a vendor.

Formula:

Outstanding Balance = Total Agreed Cost − Total Amount Paid

Example:

  • Agreed vendor cost: ₦400,000
  • Amount paid: ₦150,000
  • Outstanding balance: ₦250,000

B. Budget variance

This shows the difference between what you planned to spend and what you actually spent.

Formula:

Budget Variance = Actual Cost − Approved Budget

Example:

  • Approved budget: ₦300,000
  • Actual cost: ₦350,000
  • Budget variance: ₦50,000 over budget

A positive variance means you spent more than planned. A negative variance means you spent less.

C. Remaining event budget

This shows how much of your overall approved budget is still available after accounting for expenses.

Formula:

Remaining Budget = Total Approved Event Budget − Total Actual Expenses

For example:

  • Total approved event budget: ₦6,000,000
  • Actual expenses recorded: ₦4,200,000
  • Remaining budget: ₦1,800,000

Remember to distinguish between money already spent and money committed to outstanding vendor payments. A budget may appear healthy even when a significant balance is due soon.

8. Plan Your Cash Flow, Not Just Your Total Budget

Having enough money to cover the total cost of an event does not necessarily mean you have enough money available when payments are due.

This is a cash flow problem.

Imagine your event costs ₦5 million, but vendors require ₦2 million in deposits within the first two weeks.

If you only have ₦1 million available at that point, you may struggle to secure the services you need, even if the full event budget is eventually available.

Create a payment calendar that shows when money must be available.

For example:

  • Eight weeks before: venue deposit and initial vendor payments — ₦800,000.
  • Six weeks before: catering and decoration deposits — ₦700,000.
  • Four weeks before: marketing, logistics and equipment — ₦500,000.
  • Two weeks before: vendor balances and final arrangements — ₦1,200,000.
  • Event week: final payments and operating expenses — ₦1,800,000.

This illustrative schedule totals ₦5,000,000.

Review this schedule every week. If a payment deadline changes, update your cash flow plan immediately.

9. What to Do When Your Event Goes Over Budget

Sometimes, your actual expenses will exceed your approved budget. When this happens, avoid making decisions based on panic.

Use this process:

Step 1: Identify the source of the increase.

Is the venue more expensive than expected? Did the guest count increase? Has a vendor added extra charges?

Step 2: Separate necessary expenses from optional upgrades.

Protect the services required to deliver the event. Review optional decoration, entertainment or promotional extras first.

Step 3: Request alternative quotations.

If a vendor's price is too high, compare alternatives. Make sure you are comparing the same scope of work and service quality.

Step 4: Review your contingency fund.

Use it for genuine unexpected expenses rather than treating it as additional spending money.

Step 5: Update the budget and communicate changes.

If other organisers, clients or sponsors are involved, explain the reason for the increase and obtain approval where necessary.

The goal is not simply to spend less. It is to make sure the money available is being used where it matters most.

10. Use the Right Tools to Manage Your Event

A spreadsheet can help you monitor expenses, but managing an event involves more than financial planning.

You may also need to coordinate guests, send invitations, collect RSVPs, communicate updates and manage entry on the event day.

This is where an event management platform becomes useful.

AriyaHQ helps event organisers manage important parts of the event process, including digital invitations, guest registration, RSVP management and guest communication.

Instead of handling every guest-related activity manually, you can use Ariya to organise invitations and registration, communicate with attendees through available messaging tools and prepare for guest check-in.

For organisers handling conferences, weddings, corporate events or large celebrations, having guest management and communication organised alongside your planning process can make the work considerably easier.

Explore AriyaHQ to see how you can manage your event's guest experience.

11. Event Budgeting Mistakes to Avoid

Even with a spreadsheet, certain mistakes can make your budget unreliable.

Forgetting small expenses: Printing, delivery, transportation and miscellaneous purchases should all be recorded.

Failing to update payments: An outdated tracker can make you believe you owe more or less than you actually do.

Ignoring payment deadlines: A vendor balance due next week is more urgent than one due next month.

Using the contingency fund too early: Reserve it for unexpected expenses, not routine upgrades.

Not documenting agreements: Keep quotations, invoices, receipts and payment confirmations.

Increasing the guest count without reviewing costs: More guests can affect catering, seating, drinks, venue capacity and logistics.

Mixing personal and event funds: Keep event transactions separate so you can accurately track spending.

Frequently Asked Questions

What should an event budget include?

An event budget should include all expected expenses, vendor quotations, approved spending limits, payments made, outstanding balances, payment deadlines and a contingency fund.

How do I calculate an event budget?

Start by listing all the services and resources your event requires. Research vendor prices, obtain quotations, allocate a spending limit to each category and add a contingency reserve for unexpected costs.

What percentage should I keep for unexpected event expenses?

A starting contingency of 5%–10% of your planned expenses is commonly useful. The appropriate amount depends on the event's size, complexity and level of uncertainty.

How do I track payments to event vendors?

Create a payment tracker containing the vendor's name, agreed amount, deposit, total paid, outstanding balance, next due date and payment status. Update it after every transaction.

Can I manage an event budget with Excel or Google Sheets?

Yes. Both tools can be used to create an event budget, calculate outstanding balances, monitor spending and track vendor payments. A well-organised spreadsheet is often sufficient for small and medium-sized events.

What is the difference between an event budget and an event expense report?

An event budget is a financial plan prepared before or during the planning process. An expense report records the money actually spent. Comparing both helps you understand whether the event stayed within its approved budget.

Final Thoughts

A successful event is not necessarily the event with the biggest budget. It is the one where resources are planned carefully, payments are managed properly and unexpected expenses do not derail the entire experience.

Start with a realistic estimate, obtain written vendor quotations, record every payment and review your budget regularly.

Most importantly, do not wait until the final week to discover that your spending has exceeded what you can afford.

Use a structured event budget tracker, keep your payment deadlines visible and organise your guest management process early.

title: Conference Registration Checklist: How to Manage Speakers, Attendees and Event Check-in
excerpt: Organise conference registration, attendee categories, speaker details, confirmation messages and post-event attendance review.
author: Ariya Journal
content:
Introduction

One area that can quickly become overwhelming is conference registration.

When registrations are handled through scattered spreadsheets, email conversations and manual messages, organisers can struggle to know who has registered, who has confirmed attendance and who has actually arrived.

A structured conference registration process helps you keep everything organised, communicate effectively with attendees and create a smoother experience from registration to the final session.

In this guide, we will walk through how to organise conference registration, manage attendees and prepare an efficient check-in process.

1. Define Your Conference Registration Requirements

Before opening registration, decide what information you need from participants and how the registration process will work.

Start by answering these questions:

  • Who is the conference intended for?
  • How many attendees can the venue accommodate?
  • Will registration be free or paid?
  • Will participants register individually or through organisations?
  • Will there be different attendee categories?
  • Do participants need to select specific sessions or workshops?
  • Will speakers, sponsors and VIP guests have separate registration arrangements?

Your answers will determine the registration structure you need.

For example, a business conference might have the following attendee categories:

  • General attendee: regular conference participant.
  • VIP: attendee with designated additional access.
  • Speaker: person presenting at the conference.
  • Sponsor: supporting organisation or representative.
  • Media: approved journalists or media representatives.
  • Staff: organisers, volunteers and event personnel.

2. Create a Conference Registration Form

Your registration form is often the first interaction attendees have with your conference.

It should be simple enough to complete quickly while collecting the information you actually need.

A standard conference registration form may include:

Personal information

  • Full name
  • Email address
  • Phone number
  • Organisation or company
  • Job title

Registration details

  • Attendee category
  • Registration type
  • Session or workshop preference, if applicable
  • Dietary requirements, where relevant
  • Accessibility requirements, where relevant

Additional information

  • How the attendee heard about the conference
  • Questions for the organisers
  • Consent to receive relevant event updates

Avoid collecting information that has no clear purpose. Long forms can discourage people from completing registration.

Also, make sure your form explains how submitted information will be used and who attendees can contact if they need assistance.

3. Set Up Your Registration Categories and Ticket Structure

If your conference has different attendance options, communicate them clearly before registration opens.

For example:

  • Standard: access to general sessions.
  • VIP: general access plus clearly described benefits.
  • Student: discounted access for eligible students.
  • Group: registration for multiple participants.
  • Virtual: online participation, if offered.

If you are offering early-bird registration, specify when the offer ends and what changes afterward.

Avoid creating too many registration categories. Every additional option can make the registration process more complicated for attendees and organisers.

4. Choose a Registration Management System

For a small meeting, a spreadsheet and email may be sufficient. For a conference with many attendees, a dedicated event registration platform can make the process easier to manage.

A suitable platform should help you:

  • Collect attendee information online.
  • Organise registration records.
  • Manage attendee categories.
  • Track registration responses.
  • Send registration confirmations and updates.
  • Maintain organised guest or attendee lists.
  • Prepare for event-day check-in.

AriyaHQ provides event registration and guest management capabilities that can help organisers collect attendee information and manage their guest lists.

You can also use its digital invitations and guest communication capabilities to keep participants informed throughout the registration process.

Explore AriyaHQ when setting up your conference registration process.

5. Plan Your Registration Communication

Registration does not end when someone submits a form.

Attendees need to know whether their registration was received, what happens next and what they should do before arriving.

Create a communication plan covering the following stages:

  • When registration opens: announce the event and invite attendees to register.
  • After submission: acknowledge the registration and explain next steps.
  • If approval is required: send an approval or status update.
  • Before the conference: send reminders and arrival details.
  • On event day: provide arrival information.
  • Afterward: thank participants and maintain the relationship.

Use email for detailed information such as schedules, venue instructions and conference materials. Use SMS for concise reminders and important time-sensitive announcements.

Make sure your messages are relevant to the recipient and that communication preferences and applicable consent requirements are respected.

6. Manage Speakers and Special Guests Separately

Speakers and special guests often require more coordination than regular attendees.

They may need to submit presentation materials, confirm their availability, provide biographies and photographs, or receive specific arrival instructions.

Create a separate speaker coordination tracker.

  • Record each speaker's name, organisation and contact details.
  • Track assigned session, presentation title and confirmation status.
  • Note agreed materials, arrival details and technical or accessibility requirements.

For sponsors and VIP guests, maintain similar records with the access arrangements and benefits agreed with them.

7. Keep Your Attendee List Updated

As registrations come in, your attendee list becomes one of the most important documents for the conference.

Do not wait until the event day to organise it.

Your attendee record should include:

  • Attendee's full name.
  • Email address and phone number.
  • Organisation.
  • Registration category.
  • Registration date.
  • Confirmation status.
  • Special requirements, where applicable.
  • Check-in status.

It is also useful to distinguish between people who registered, people whose attendance has been confirmed and people who actually arrived.

These are three different stages.

For example, a person may complete registration but fail to attend the conference. Someone else may register and confirm attendance but arrive late.

Keeping these statuses separate gives organisers a more accurate picture of attendance.

8. Coordinate registration with the event-day check-in plan

Registration happens before the conference; check-in verifies attendees when they arrive. Share the confirmed attendee list, categories and authorised exception process with the check-in lead. For queue planning, staff roles and arrival problems, use our event check-in guide.

9. Track Attendance and Evaluate Your Registration Process

Once the conference is over, review the registration and attendance information.

This helps you understand what worked, what needs improvement and how to plan future conferences.

Useful figures to review include:

Total registrations: How many people registered?

Confirmed attendees: How many participants confirmed that they intended to attend?

Actual attendance: How many people checked in?

Attendance rate: What percentage of registered participants attended?

You can calculate attendance rate using:

Attendance Rate = (Actual Attendees ÷ Total Registrations) × 100

For example:

  • Total registrations: 500
  • Actual attendees: 400
  • Attendance rate: 80%

This means 80% of registered participants attended the conference.

Also review common registration questions, check-in delays, communication problems and feedback from attendees.

These findings can help you improve the experience at your next event.

Conference Registration Checklist

Use this checklist to review your preparations before opening registration and before the conference begins.

Before registration opens

  • Define the conference audience and attendance capacity.
  • Decide on registration categories.
  • Set registration deadlines.
  • Prepare the registration form.
  • Confirm the registration platform.
  • Prepare registration confirmation messages.
  • Set up speaker and sponsor records.
  • Test the registration process.

After registration opens

  • Monitor new registrations.
  • Review attendee information.
  • Follow up on incomplete or pending registrations.
  • Send relevant confirmations.
  • Share conference updates.
  • Coordinate speakers and special guests.
  • Prepare attendee lists.

Before the conference

  • Finalise the registration records.
  • Prepare QR code passes where applicable.
  • Assign check-in staff.
  • Organise registration desks.
  • Test QR code scanning.
  • Prepare backup check-in arrangements.
  • Share arrival instructions.
  • Confirm speaker and VIP arrangements.

On the conference day

  • Set up registration desks and signage.
  • Brief registration staff.
  • Verify attendee registrations.
  • Manage queues.
  • Record attendee check-ins.
  • Resolve registration issues.
  • Direct attendees to the appropriate areas.

After the conference

  • Review actual attendance.
  • Calculate attendance rate.
  • Send thank-you messages.
  • Collect attendee feedback.
  • Review registration challenges.
  • Document lessons for future conferences.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is conference registration management?

Conference registration management is the process of collecting attendee information, organising registrations, confirming participation, communicating with participants and preparing them for event-day entry.

What information should a conference registration form collect?

A standard form should collect the attendee's name, email address, phone number, organisation, job title and registration category. Additional fields can include session preferences, accessibility requirements and dietary information where relevant.

What is the best way to manage conference registration?

For conferences with many participants, a dedicated registration platform is usually more efficient than managing everything manually. Look for a solution that supports online registration, attendee records, confirmations, communication and check-in preparation.

How do I prevent long queues at conference registration?

Use organised registration desks, assign sufficient staff, separate attendee categories where necessary and consider QR code check-in. Test your process before the event and prepare a backup for technical problems.

How do I manage conference speakers and VIP guests?

Maintain separate records for speakers and VIPs. Track their contact details, session assignments, confirmations, presentation requirements, arrival instructions and any special access arrangements.

Can QR codes be used for conference registration?

Yes. QR codes can be issued as digital passes to registered attendees and used during check-in to help staff identify and verify participants through a compatible system.

Final Thoughts

Conference registration is not just about collecting names. It is about creating an organised process that connects registration, communication, attendee management and event-day access.

When these activities are planned properly, organisers spend less time resolving avoidable problems and more time delivering a successful conference.

Start by creating a clear registration process, keeping your attendee records updated and preparing your check-in team well ahead of the event.

title: Event Planning for Agencies: How to Manage Multiple Clients and Events at Once
excerpt: Create repeatable workflows for agency projects, client communication, deadlines, vendors and separate event guest lists.
imageAlt: Event team reviewing guest and project information together on laptops
author: Ariya Journal
content:
Introduction

You could be coordinating a corporate conference for one client, planning a wedding for another, organising a product launch and preparing a private celebration, all within the same month.

Each event has its own client, budget, vendors, guest list, deadlines and expectations.

As your agency grows, managing everything through scattered WhatsApp conversations, spreadsheets, notebooks and email threads becomes increasingly difficult. Important details can get lost, deadlines can overlap and your team may struggle to know what needs attention.

The solution is to create a repeatable system for managing multiple events.

In this guide, we will explore how event planning agencies can organise several client projects, coordinate their teams, manage guest information and maintain control as their workload grows.

1. Treat Every Client Event as a Separate Project

One of the biggest mistakes an event agency can make is managing all its events as though they are part of one large project.

Although your team may work on several events simultaneously, every client engagement should have its own project record.

For each event, create a central record containing:

  • Client name and contact information.
  • Event name and type.
  • Event date and location.
  • Agreed scope of work.
  • Approved budget.
  • Assigned team members.
  • Vendor information.
  • Important deadlines.
  • Guest and registration requirements.
  • Outstanding tasks and decisions.

For example, an agency managing three events could organise its work like this:

  • Project Alpha: Company A; 12 December; lead Sarah; in progress.
  • Project Beta: Client B; 19 December; lead Daniel; awaiting approval.
  • Project Gamma: Company C; 10 January; lead Michael; planning.

The rule is simple: every event should have one central source of information.

2. Build a Repeatable Event Planning Workflow

Your agency should not have to invent a new planning process every time it gets a client.

Create a standard workflow that can be adapted to different event types.

A practical agency workflow can be divided into six stages.

Stage 1: Client onboarding

  • Understand the client's objectives.
  • Confirm the event type and expected attendance.
  • Discuss the budget.
  • Agree on responsibilities.
  • Document the scope of work.
  • Confirm important dates and expectations.

Stage 2: Event planning

  • Develop the event plan.
  • Research and contact vendors.
  • Compare quotations.
  • Confirm the venue.
  • Prepare the event schedule.
  • Identify operational requirements.

Stage 3: Registration and guest management

  • Prepare invitations.
  • Set up registration.
  • Organise the guest list.
  • Monitor RSVP responses.
  • Prepare attendee communication.
  • Organise guest access arrangements.

Stage 4: Event preparation

  • Confirm vendors.
  • Review outstanding payments.
  • Finalise the programme.
  • Brief staff and suppliers.
  • Prepare registration and check-in arrangements.
  • Confirm final guest numbers.

Stage 5: Event execution

  • Coordinate vendors and staff.
  • Manage guest arrivals.
  • Monitor the programme.
  • Handle unexpected issues.
  • Keep the client informed.

Stage 6: Post-event delivery

  • Complete outstanding deliverables.
  • Share agreed photographs or reports.
  • Collect client feedback.
  • Review event performance.
  • Record lessons for future projects.

You can use this workflow as the foundation for every new client project, adjusting it based on the event's size and complexity.

3. Create a Central Task and Deadline Tracker

When managing multiple events, remembering every deadline becomes difficult.

A vendor may need confirmation for one event while another client is waiting for a proposal. At the same time, your team may be preparing invitations for an upcoming celebration.

Without a shared task tracker, people can easily overlook responsibilities.

Create a task tracker with these columns:

  • Project Alpha: confirm venue; Sarah; 25 November; high priority; pending.
  • Project Alpha: approve invitation design; Daniel; 27 November; medium priority; in progress.
  • Project Beta: finalise guest list; Michael; 29 November; high priority; pending.
  • Project Gamma: request catering quotes; Sarah; 2 December; medium priority; completed.
  • A clear description.
  • One person responsible.
  • A deadline.
  • A priority level.
  • A status.

Avoid assigning vague responsibilities such as "handle event planning". Break large responsibilities into smaller tasks that can be completed and tracked.

It is also important to review the tracker regularly. A task management system only works when your team keeps it updated.

4. Assign Clear Responsibilities to Your Team

As your agency takes on more clients, the founder or lead planner should not have to manage every detail personally.

Assign responsibilities according to your team's structure and the needs of each event.

For example:

  • Account manager: client communication and expectations.
  • Project manager: event coordination and deadlines.
  • Vendor coordinator: sourcing, quotes and confirmations.
  • Guest-management officer: invitations, registration and attendee records.
  • Marketing officer: event promotion and communication.
  • Operations team: venue, logistics and event-day execution.

For every event, appoint a project lead who is accountable for keeping the project on track.

This reduces confusion when several team members are involved in the same client engagement.

5. Keep Every Client's Communication Separate

Client communication can become one of the most difficult parts of managing an event agency.

You may receive instructions through WhatsApp, approvals through email, phone calls from vendors and last-minute changes during meetings.

If decisions are not documented, important information can easily be forgotten.

Create a communication record for every client.

It should include:

  • Client instructions.
  • Important decisions.
  • Approved designs and documents.
  • Changes to the event requirements.
  • Confirmed vendor arrangements.
  • Outstanding questions.
  • Agreed deadlines.

After important meetings or phone calls, send a short written summary of what was agreed.

For example:

Meeting summary – Project Alpha

  • Venue: Approved.
  • Catering: Client reviewing two quotations.
  • Invitation design: Second draft requested.
  • Guest registration: Expected to open on 1 December.
  • Next review meeting: 28 November.

This gives your team a clear reference point and helps prevent disagreements about what was agreed.

You should also establish a preferred communication channel with each client. Avoid allowing critical approvals to remain buried in personal conversations.

6. Manage Guest Lists and Registrations for Each Event

Guest management becomes more complicated when your agency is handling several events.

One client may have 150 invited guests, another may expect 500 conference participants, while a third may require a controlled VIP guest list.

Using one unstructured spreadsheet for every client creates unnecessary risks.

Instead, maintain separate guest records for each event.

Each event's guest list may include:

  • Full name.
  • Email address.
  • Phone number.
  • Invitation status.
  • RSVP response.
  • Guest category.
  • Number of additional guests, where permitted.
  • Registration status.
  • Check-in status.

Also establish clear access controls for your team. Staff should only access client information when their responsibilities require it.
